extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media researchers, newsroom editors/managers, and policymakers interested in news content and democratic effects
extracted.subtask_description: A content-analysis coding scheme and conceptual rubric for evaluating news stories (1980–1999) focused on distinguishing soft vs. hard news, frames, style, topic, and other story-level attributes. Includes operational definitions, code values, and coding guidance used in a large-scale content analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEWS SECTION
rubrics_metrics.description: Which section of the outlet the story appears in (e.g., 1/A/National; 2/B/Metro; Other; Indeterminate section (newspaper); Television News).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code the news section placement; with television code as 'Television News'.

rubrics_metrics.name: STORY SOURCE (byline/wire/compiled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Source type of the story: news outlet byline story; news outlet, no byline; news outlet’s wire service; compiled from wire services; AP; Reuters/UPI; NYT or other outlet-based wire service; other identified source; source not identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code which of the listed source categories produced the story; distinguish wire vs. original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: STORY LOCATION / PLACEMENT
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of the story (page number or order in newscast). For television, placement is based on story order in the newscast (count from top or bottom as instructed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with outlets that load backwards (e.g., NBC); count order accordingly; code page/top-of-newscast position.

rubrics_metrics.name: STORY LENGTH
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of the story measured in words (4-digit); with special codes for indeterminate or exceeding maximum (e.g., 9998, 9999).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If story exceeds 9998 words code as 9998; use 9999 for indeterminate length.

rubrics_metrics.name: DAY OF WEEK
rubrics_metrics.description: Day of week the story appeared (Monday–Sunday).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code 1=Monday, 2=Tuesday, ... 7=Sunday.

rubrics_metrics.name: TYPE OF STORY
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize lead/type of story (focus on the lead): Basically straight news/hard news (happened in past 24 hours; event/incident based); Balanced mix of straight news and news analysis; Mainly news analysis (includes motives, expectations); Feature/human interest; Verbatim text/interview/speech/document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine type by the story's leading component; code as one of the defined types.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOCUS OF STORY
rubrics_metrics.description: Key focus/peg of the story: Current/ongoing event or development; Current incident (an isolated personal event, e.g., a crime); Update on past event; Update on past incident; Upcoming event; Non-event/non-incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus may be current even if peg is retrospective; classify whether story centers on event vs. incident vs. non-event.

rubrics_metrics.name: SALIENCE OF STORY
rubrics_metrics.description: Why the story is in today's news — magnitude/timeliness salience scale (1–5): from must-cover-on-this-day events to small-magnitude items an editor could choose to cover or ignore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided scale (1 highest salience—no responsible editor could ignore; 5 small magnitude/choice to cover).

rubrics_metrics.name: SOURCE OF STORY (origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the story originated: outside event/incident triggered it; inside decision (editor/reporter) triggered it; cannot be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish stories generated by external events versus internal newsroom initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: PUBLIC/PRIVATE FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether story is framed in the public realm or private realm: Public affairs/public realm (includes public actors or public-affairs without public actor, e.g., a criminal act with public-safety implications); Private realm involving a salient actor (celebrity, corporation, foundation) or purely private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code based on whether the story concerns public affairs/public actors vs. private/celebrity/private institution focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: POLICY / NON-POLICY FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story have relevance for public policy? Options: substantially policy related/policy relevant; somewhat policy related; non-policy related (or inconsequential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all public affairs are policy relevant; policy relevance must be stated (e.g., a crime story with no reference to public safety may be non-policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: ACTION / NON-ACTION FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story implies/indicates a need for action and its urgency: (1) implies urgent need for action/indicates problem needs fixing; (2) implies a non-urgent need for action; (3) describes action already taken/being taken; (4) no action component of note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use attribution codes if action/non-action present; determine if story suggests who should act.

rubrics_metrics.name: ATTRIBUTION OF RESPONSIBILITY FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Who/what is portrayed as responsible for addressing the issue (applies if action frame coded 1–3): government/level of government/public official; a group/collective/community/private institution; private individual; not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which actor is implied/explicitly assigned responsibility for the problem/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEWS YOU CAN USE (practical advice purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the story's primary purpose to offer personal-level advice (e.g., health or money advice)? Code: primary purpose; secondary purpose; not the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish stories aimed at giving actionable personal advice from other functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONTEXTUAL FRAME (episodic vs. thematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is episodic (case-study, focused on particular event/incident) or thematic (places issue in broader context/trend/implications for society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code episodic when the story centers on a single event without broader context; thematic when it explains societal meaning or trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONFLICT / NON-CONFLICT FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the story presents conflict: substantial level of conflict; some conflict (not merely incidental); no/insignificant conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge presentation style and content to determine conflict level.

rubrics_metrics.name: NATURE OF CONFLICT
rubrics_metrics.description: If conflict is present, classify it as actual conflict (real, observable conflict between participants) or synthetic conflict (conflict chiefly constructed/introduced by the reporter via juxtaposition/speculation), or cannot determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only code if conflict code is 1 or 2; decide whether conflict is reporter-imposed or genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: HUMAN-INTEREST FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which story uses a human example/puts a human face on an issue or probes private/personal life: High human interest; Moderate; Slight; None (incidental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest stories use personal vignettes, sympathy/empathy cues; code degree accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEGATIVE / POSITIVE FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall valence of the story (good/bad for subject/society): 1=Clearly negative/unfavorable/bad news; 2=More negative than positive; 3=Balanced mix; 4=More positive than negative; 5=Clearly positive/favorable/good news; 6=Neutral/no valence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a press secretary would see story as favorable/unfavorable; apply at story level.

rubrics_metrics.name: SENSATIONALISM FRAME
rubrics_metrics.description: Breathlessness/hype quality of the story as presented by the journalist: High sensationalism; Moderate sensationalism; Low sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reporter's framing, adjective use, and hype rather than substance; determine whether story is 'hyped'.

rubrics_metrics.name: STORY AMBIANCE (tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone of the story irrespective of topic: Serious/Important; Matter of fact; Lighthearted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code the overall tone conveyed by the writing/presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: JOURNALISTIC STYLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic mode of reporting: Descriptive (tells 'what' happened straightforwardly) versus Interpretive/analytical/evaluative (analyzes, evaluates or explains while describing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the story contains evaluation/explanation versus pure description.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOFT NEWS / HARD NEWS (classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall categorization of the story along the soft/hard continuum: Definitely a soft news story; Mostly a soft news story; Mixed rather evenly; Mostly a hard news story; Definitely a hard news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes the report's central construct: soft news defined in part as stories without clear connection to policy; also consider characteristics (sensational, human-interest, incident-based).

rubrics_metrics.name: GEOGRAPHIC ARENA
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic scale/location of the story: Foreign/international (no US component); Foreign/international with significant US component; National with significant foreign link; National; Regional (multi-state); State; Local; None/no location context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code based on location context and relevance to U.S. component where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: STORY LEAD (type of lead/person presented)
rubrics_metrics.description: What leads the story: A political/governmental personality (newsmaker/political leader/celebrity); Nonpolitical/nongovernmental personality; Expert person (professor, economist, doctor); Ordinary/unknown person; Institution or agency of government; Group/organization; Corporation/business-related entity; Country/State/City.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume person is newsworthy because of role; code the lead actor type accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAIN ACTOR / REALM CODE
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific realm of main actor where applicable: President/White House/Administration; Cabinet Officer/federal agency; Member of Congress/Congress; Supreme Court/federal judiciary; etc.; or Not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use main-actor codes consistent with previous story-lead codes; apply when actor is a public/governmental figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAJOR TOPIC CODE
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary topical domain of the story (wide taxonomy): Government & policy; Politics (campaigns/vote/strategy); Political scandal; Political personality; Business & commerce; Celebrity; Celebrity crime/scandal; Crime; Natural disasters; Manmade disasters; Science; Technology; Medicine; Personal health; Media; Entertainment/Arts/Fashion/Travel; Food; Religion; Sports; Legal affairs; Education; Stock Market; and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the single best-fit major topic code from the detailed list provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAJOR ISSUE CODE
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific issue-category within broader topics: natural/manmade tragedy; entertainment/arts/lifestyle; sports; business; economy; unemployment/jobs; international trade; environment; labor/wages; agriculture; taxes; government spending; health; welfare; education; consumers; housing; transportation; social security; family/children; public safety; war/peace; terrorism; national defense; foreign affairs; immigration; famine; genocide; race/women/abortion/etc.; crime (as broad problem); drugs; police conduct; criminal justice system; science; technology (policy); communications (policy); religion; performance of government/media/business; condition of society; campaign finance; and many more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific issue codes to capture policy-relevant content; refer to memo sheet when an 'other' category is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAJOR CONTEXT FRAME (story framing types)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the story is framed overall: Ambition and power (winning/losing/strategy); Conflict frame (blame/infighting/differences); Cooperation frame (working together/collective effort); Problem/policy frame (identifying/explaining problems or policy solutions); Human interest frame; None of these (describe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the principal contextual frame that organizes the story's presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: DICTION-BASED VOCABULARY MEASURES
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual/vocabulary measures derived from DICTION categories used to indicate style/softness or hardness: COLLECTIVES (categorical/social grouping words), SELF-REFERENCE (first-person references), HUMAN INTEREST (personal pronouns, family words), COMPLEXITY (average word length), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DICTION computer program outputs to measure changes in vocabulary consistent with soft/hard news (e.g., declines in COLLECTIVES, increases in SELF-REFERENCE and HUMAN INTEREST).

rubrics_metrics.name: SOFT NEWS CHARACTERISTICS (operational indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics commonly used to identify soft news: more sensational; more personality-centered; less time-bound; more practical (news you can use); more incident-based; higher human-interest content; dramatic incidents (crime/disaster); and a more personal/familiar vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics are used conceptually and operationally (via coding frames such as sensationalism, human-interest, public/policy frame, and DICTION measures) to classify soft vs. hard stories.
